questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why do amino acids exist as zwitterions rather than as neutral NH2-COOH molecules?

answer.exemplar: The carboxyl group is acidic enough to transfer a proton to the basic amino group, forming a carboxylate and an ammonium ion; this internal acid-base reaction is favored because the resulting ionic form is stabilized by solvation in polar water and by the strong electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges.

questions.explanation: Internal proton transfer is thermodynamically favorable. The carboxyl group is acidic enough to transfer a proton to the basic amino group, forming a carboxylate and an ammonium ion; this internal acid-base reaction is favored because the resulting ionic form is stabilized by solvation in polar water and by the strong electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the pI of a simple amino acid the average of its two pKa values?

answer.exemplar: Between the first and second deprotonations the zwitterion is the dominant species, and it is exactly at the midpoint in pH between the pKa of the ammonium group and the pKa of the carboxyl group that the concentrations of the cationic and anionic forms become equal, giving net zero charge; for simple amino acids this midpoint is the average of the two pKa values.

questions.explanation: The neutral zwitterion dominates between the two pKas. Between the first and second deprotonations the zwitterion is the dominant species, and it is exactly at the midpoint in pH between the pKa of the ammonium group and the pKa of the carboxyl group that the concentrations of the cationic and anionic forms become equal, giving net zero charge; for simple amino acids this midpoint is the average of the two pKa values.
questions.hint: Equal positive and negative forms at the pI.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the peptide bond planar and rigid?

answer.exemplar: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl pi system, giving the carbon-nitrogen bond partial double-bond character that restricts rotation; as a result the six atoms of the peptide unit lie in one plane, with trans arrangement of substituents usually favored for steric reasons.

questions.explanation: Resonance gives partial double-bond character. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl pi system, giving the carbon-nitrogen bond partial double-bond character that restricts rotation; as a result the six atoms of the peptide unit lie in one plane, with trans arrangement of substituents usually favored for steric reasons.
questions.hint: Rotation about the C-N bond is restricted.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does Edman degradation allow sequencing from the N-terminus without destroying the rest of the peptide?

answer.exemplar: The reagent reacts selectively with the free N-terminal amino group under mildly basic conditions, and acid cleavage then removes only that single labeled residue as a stable derivative while leaving all remaining peptide bonds intact, so the shortened peptide can undergo another cycle.

questions.explanation: Only the N-terminal residue is labeled and cleaved. The reagent reacts selectively with the free N-terminal amino group under mildly basic conditions, and acid cleavage then removes only that single labeled residue as a stable derivative while leaving all remaining peptide bonds intact, so the shortened peptide can undergo another cycle.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Provide the explanation: why is the peptide bond planar and rigid?

answer.exemplar: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl pi system, giving the carbon-nitrogen bond partial double-bond character that restricts rotation; as a result the six atoms of the peptide unit lie in one plane, with trans arrangement of substituents usually favored for steric reasons.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Provide the explanation: why does Edman degradation allow sequencing from the N-terminus without destroying the rest of the peptide?

answer.exemplar: The reagent reacts selectively with the free N-terminal amino group under mildly basic conditions, and acid cleavage then removes only that single labeled residue as a stable derivative while leaving all remaining peptide bonds intact, so the shortened peptide can undergo another cycle.
